items.title: Gus Fontenet Interview
items.q: INTERVIEWER: Do you recall the names of any of the outstanding colored musicians that are in this area or in New Orleans who worked with white musicians to teach them how to play Dixieland? ... Emanuel Manetta in New Orleans. He taught quite a few.

ctx.x: I think rock and roll is somewhat on the same footing as this bebop that they had it. It was out in a blast for a while and all of a sudden it just died out. That rock and roll I don't think it'll last too long either. It might but I doubt it.

I noticed some of the numbers on the jukebox now they're kind of getting away from rock and roll some of the numbers. Some people seem to think that rock and roll is less but I don't. It's kind of hard to say. Why would you say that the Dixieland style seems to be the most lasting of all? Is there any special reason that you would have been on? I think I think and there was more music. A musician at that time had to learn to execute his instrument more than the, the, with this rock and roll. Yeah there's not…

around here ever came in and then sat on your combos and their playing for these various dances? No, they didn't. Not out here. Well, how did these white musicians that like jazz, like Dixieland, show their interest in this? They would come to the dances in different places and listen. They would follow you around in from one place to another. Yes.
